topic: Medicine began with herbs, rituals and surgery such as trepanation; Egypt, Mesopotamia, India and China developed written medical traditions.
Greek medicine (Hippocrates, Galen) explained disease by the four humours, a theory that lasted until the 19th century.
Islamic physicians preserved and extended Greek medicine; Renaissance anatomy (Vesalius) and Harvey's circulation of the blood began modern medicine.
Germ theory, anaesthesia, antiseptics, vaccines and antibiotics transformed medicine from the 19th century and greatly extended life expectancy.

Prehistoric medicine: Prehistoric healing relied on medicinal plants, rituals and practical care.
Trepanation, drilling holes in the skull, was practised from at least 7000 BC, and many patients survived.
Plant remedies were learned by trial and passed on orally.
Ancient Mesopotamian medicine: Mesopotamian healers were of two kinds: the asû (physician, using herbs) and the āšipu (exorcist, using rituals).
Disease was often blamed on gods, demons or sin.
The Diagnostic Handbook (about 1050 BC) records symptoms and prognoses systematically.
Ancient Egyptian medicine: Egyptian physicians were famous across the ancient world; Imhotep was later worshipped as a god of medicine.
The Edwin Smith Papyrus describes injuries and surgery rationally; the Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BC) lists hundreds of remedies.
Physicians specialised, according to Herodotus, in particular body parts or diseases.
Ancient Chinese medicine: Traditional Chinese medicine took shape from the Zhou dynasty onward.
The 'Huangdi Neijing' (Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic) explains health as the balance of yin and yang and the flow of qi.
Treatments included herbs, acupuncture and moxibustion.
Ancient Indian medicine: The Atharvaveda contains charms and herbal remedies against disease.
Ayurveda explains health by the balance of three doshas.
The Charaka Samhita covers internal medicine; the Sushruta Samhita describes surgery, including plastic surgery of the nose.
Ancient Greek medicine: Hippocrates (5th century BC) sought natural causes of disease and stressed observation; the Hippocratic Oath bears his name.
Disease was explained by an imbalance of four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.
Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies in Alexandria.
Galen's writings (2nd century) dominated Western medicine until the 17th century.
Ancient Roman medicine: Romans invented many surgical instruments, including forceps, scalpels and specula, and performed cataract surgery.
Dioscorides' 'De materia medica' was the standard guide to medicinal plants for 1,500 years.
Roman public health, with aqueducts, baths and sewers, and military hospitals, was advanced.
Post-classical medicine: Byzantine medicine preserved Greco-Roman knowledge; physicians such as Paul of Aegina compiled it.
Islamic scholars such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek texts; Al-Razi distinguished smallpox from measles.
Avicenna's 'Canon of Medicine' (1025) was a standard textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.
Hospitals (bimaristans) spread across the Islamic world, and medical schools at Salerno and Montpellier arose in Europe.
Early modern medicine: Vesalius's anatomy (1543) corrected Galen through dissection.
William Harvey showed that blood circulates (1628).
European diseases such as smallpox devastated the Americas after 1492.
Edward Jenner introduced smallpox vaccination in 1796.
Late modern medicine: Pasteur and Koch established the germ theory of disease and identified the bacteria behind diseases such as tuberculosis and cholera.
Anaesthesia (1840s) and Lister's antiseptic surgery (1867) made surgery far safer.
Florence Nightingale reformed nursing; Landsteiner discovered blood groups (1901), making transfusion safe.
Fleming discovered penicillin (1928); the 1918 influenza pandemic killed tens of millions.
Contemporary medicine: Antibiotics made infections curable and enabled organ transplants and open-heart surgery; resistance to them is a growing threat.
HIV/AIDS, identified in the 1980s, and the COVID-19 pandemic (from 2019) were the major modern pandemics; mRNA vaccines were developed rapidly against COVID-19.
Robotics, telemedicine and personalised (genome-based) medicine are recent developments.
Themes in medical history: Racism has shaped medicine, through unequal treatment and scientific racism.
Women long practised as healers and midwives but were excluded from universities and medical schools.
Elizabeth Blackwell became the first woman to earn a medical degree in the United States, in 1849.
